sentences.text: Departure metering extends the restriction handling process by deciding where delay is best absorbed before aircraft begin taxi.
The Departure Metering Service, known operationally as Emberline, is the system function that converts runway demand into controlled stand delay before aircraft enter the taxi stream.
The metering process starts when the Regional Flow Platform normalizes each Flight Intent Message against the current Airport Capacity Plan.
The Demand Prediction Service estimates the departure demand profile by stand, apron area, runway, and departure fix.
The Capacity Assessment Module compares that demand with the active Airport Acceptance Rate, runway configuration, taxiway constraints, and sector limits.
The Departure Metering Service then derives a feasible Target Off Block Time that protects the Calculated Takeoff Time without overloading the surface movement area.
Stand absorption is preferred when the aircraft can remain connected to normal operator processes and when holding at the gate will not create a gate conflict.
Pushback windows are coordinated as narrow time bands that give the flight crew, ramp team, and tower sequence a common expectation without treating the window as a clearance to move.
Blueharbor shall adjust allocated departure times when metering rules require additional stand absorption to preserve the planned runway sequence.
Halcyon records the agreed pushback window rationale in the coordination notes before the plan is released to operational users.
The Ramp Control Lead reviews the proposed windows against apron congestion, towing activity, and aircraft readiness before accepting them for local execution.
The Tower Supervisor monitors whether the planned release rate remains compatible with departure spacing and runway crossing demand.
The North Runway Meter and South Runway Meter maintain independent queue counts so that one runway cannot mask an excess queue on the other runway.
Surface surveillance inputs from the Surface Surveillance Adapter are used to confirm the actual number of aircraft waiting at runway holding points.
The Ramp Movement Board produces the Fuel Truck Hold Advice when metering decisions require servicing activity to remain clear of an aircraft that is being held at stand.
The Airline Operations Coordinator confirms whether each affected aircraft can absorb the assigned delay at stand without compromising crew, passenger, or turnaround constraints.
If an operator cannot accept the proposed stand delay, the Aircraft Operator Representative requests reconsideration through the Airport CDM Portal.
The Gate Conflict Detector warns when continued stand holding would block an inbound allocation or create a conflict with a planned equipment move.
Business Rules Registry parameters define the maximum planned runway queue, the warning threshold, and the intervention threshold for each runway configuration.
When a predicted queue exceeds the warning threshold, the Alert Distribution Hub highlights the affected runway queue on the Common Situation Display.
During Adverse Weather Mode, the Regional Flow Manager may increase stand absorption to prevent unstable taxi queues from forming under reduced visibility or wet surface conditions.

In a Capacity Reduction State, the Airport Duty Manager and Tower Supervisor agree whether the metering horizon should be extended so that delay is absorbed before pushback rather than near the runway.
All changes to Target Off Block Time values, Calculated Takeoff Time values, and threshold overrides are written to the Collaborative Decision Log and Audit Event Ledger.
The Performance Analytics Warehouse later compares planned stand absorption, actual off block performance, and runway queue length to verify that the agreed thresholds were not exceeded.
